item.title: C++ Rvalue Reference Return Best Practices and Pitfalls
item.description:
“C++ Rvalue Reference Return Best Practices and Pitfalls”

When dealing with function returns involving large objects like std::vector in modern C++, developers often look to move semantics (rvalue references, &&) for performance gains. However, misusing them can lead to serious runtime errors. What are the correct patterns for returning objects by value versus using rvalue references, and what are the associated safety implications?

Let’s examine several scenarios involving a function that returns a std::vector<int> initialized locally.

item.title: C++ Rvalue References in Function Returns Best Practices
item.description:
“C++ Rvalue References in Function Returns Best Practices”

When dealing with modern C++ and returning complex objects like containers, precisely how one captures the return value—especially involving rvalue references (&&)—significantly impacts performance and correctness. How should we structure functions that return objects, and what are the pitfalls of binding the result to a named rvalue reference?

Let’s examine several coding patterns when a function returns a concrete value versus when it might attempt to return a reference.

item.title: C++ std::vector Reallocation Avoiding Copies: Enforcing Move Semantics
item.description:
“C++ std::vector Reallocation Avoiding Copies: Enforcing Move Semantics”

When std::vector needs to grow its underlying array, it often results in reallocation. During this process, existing elements must be transferred to the new memory location. A primary concern in performance-critical C++ code is ensuring the container leverages move semantics over costly copy operations. Why is the move constructor sometimes skipped in favor of a copy, even when a move constructor is defined?
